catalog_quote: [Rice 1990: 221] A phonetic distinction in vowel prominence is found in Hare. In particular, the prestem vowel in verbs is phonetically more prominent, having greater stress and fuller vowel quality, than the stem vowel. ... The prestem syllable retains its prominence even if it is preceded by another syllable. [p. 222] In (31), [wah], the prestem syllable, is the most prominent syllable in the word. Prominence distinctions thus are found within the familiar domain of the foot. The prominence of the left-hand vowel supports the hypothesis put forth in section 3.3 that the left branch of the verbal foot is strong as it is the left branch that is more prominent. ... Even when the stem vowel is not lost, it is often quite low in prominence when it is utterance-final. [p. 224] Parallel prominence distinctions occur in Bearlake; however, the stem vowel is more intense than the prestem vowel. Stem vowel deletion and the dramatic tone shift effect found in Hare verbs are not present in Bearlake. This is to be expected given that prominence facts in Bearlake suggest that the foot has a strong right branch rather than a strong left branch. [p. 230] (45c, d) show nouns contrasting with related verb forms where the stem vowel is prominent in the noun and the prestem syllable in the related verb: (45c) ʔɛk'a 'fat' cf. lɛk'a 'it is fat' (45d) godih 'large game animals' cf. gode 's/he talks, speaks'
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: North Slavey (nort2942) is not in the catalog. Of the three title-hit items, two (Rice 1987 typescript; Rice 1990 Lingua) are first-hand studies of word-level prominence in the Hare dialect and were obtained in full: the Alaska Native Language Archive serves the PDFs from its Online/ directory (https://uafanlc.alaska.edu/Online/CA976Rc1987/Metrical-Structure.PDF., plus the 1993 Sketch of Slave, which has no stress statement); the record pages do not advertise them. Both state that in Hare verbs the prestem syllable is the most prominent syllable ('greater stress and fuller vowel quality'), that in nouns/postpositions the stem syllable is prominent, and (1990, p. 224) that in Bearlake the stem vowel is more intense than the prestem vowel; the correlate is intensity/duration, not pitch, and stress is not distinctive. This matches the Rice 1989 grammar sec. 4.4 passage reconstructed from search-inside windows by the earlier reading. Savishinsky 1974 is an ethnography (psychological stress) and irrelevant. Two further paywalled Rice papers (2005 Athabaskan Prosody ch; 2018 CUP ch.) were found in bibliographic records and are medium-priority acquisitions but not needed for the classification. all lookups were done by automated download/direct download.

new_statements.quote: 4.4 Stress. Stress is not a distinctive feature [in] Slave. In the Hare dialect, there are stress-like properties which are predictable. What might be called stress generally falls on the vowel immediately preceding the stem of a verb and on the stem vowel of a noun. A stressed vowel is generally acoustically more intense than an unstressed vowel, and intensity is in fact the primary phonetic correlate of stress. See chapter 8. In prefixes in all dialects, a high tone may fall on a vowel with lexical high tone. That vowel then has extra stress, or is more intense.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Slave is a tone language and stress is not contrastive. In the Hare dialect (Fort Good Hope / Colville Lake, a North Slavey dialect) there is predictable prominence: in verbs it falls on the vowel immediately preceding the verb stem (the last prefix syllable), in nouns on the stem vowel; the acoustic cue is intensity. In all dialects a prefix vowel carrying lexical high tone is more intense ('extra stress'). No positional rule is given for Bearlake, Mountain or (South) Slavey beyond the tone-linked intensity remark.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the windows read; the only additional prominence noted is 'extra stress' (greater intensity) on prefix vowels with lexical high tone, in all dialects.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated in the windows read ('generally falls'); the passage continues with examples (77) that were not retrievable through the snippet windows.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (verb word: pre-stem prefix vowel; noun: stem vowel). Ch. 8 adds that Hare has high tone on the vowel preceding the verb stem and low tone on the stem itself, i.e. the Hare prominence site coincides with the shifted tone site. Text reconstructed verbatim by chaining overlapping search-inside scanned windows; 'feature Slave' is scanned (probably 'feature in Slave' or 'of Slave'); example forms and the rest of p.46 not seen.
new_statements.identity_note: Rice 1989 'Slave' covers four dialects: Slavey (= South Slavey, sout2959), Bearlake, Hare and Mountain (the latter three = North Slavey nort2942). The stress statement is explicitly about the Hare dialect (Fort Good Hope / Colville Lake; Glottolog dialect under nort2942, code not verified), with only the tone-linked 'extra stress' remark applying to all dialects; no positional rule is given for Bearlake or Mountain.

new_statements.reading: North Slavey has no contrastive word stress (tone is contrastive). Prominence is predictable and anchored to the morphological stem, not to a word edge: in Hare verbs the syllable immediately preceding the stem is the strongest in the word (left-strong foot built at the stem; the stem vowel is weak and may delete utterance-finally), while in Hare nouns and postpositions the stem (final) syllable is strongest (right-strong foot). In the Bearlake dialect the stem vowel is the more intense one in verbs too. The phonetic correlate is intensity (perhaps duration), not pitch (Rice 1987 fn. 5). For catalog purposes: morphologically conditioned (stem-relative) prominence, with a Hare-verb 'pre-stem' vs. Bearlake/noun 'stem-final' split. This agrees with the Rice 1989 Grammar of Slave sec. 4.4 passage reconstructed held by the project by the earlier reading ('Stress is not a distinctive feature [in] Slave.. falls on the vowel immediately preceding the stem of a verb and on the stem vowel of a noun'), which remains the most general single statement but was not directly readable.

tone_statements.quote: The basic C-H pattern with high tone from constriction or glottalization, and low tone in its absence, has been called “high-marked” … The acute or high-marked area includes Chipewyan, Beaver, Slave, Kaska, Northern Tutchone, Hare-Bearlake-Mountain, and also Chilcotin. … Hare, Mountain, Bearlake and Slave, closely related and largely mutually intelligible, all show very regular development of high-marked tone. In Hare the stem-tone assimilates to that of the suffix, but in Bearlake and Slavey there is no such assimilation … Mountain appears tonally identical with Bearlake.

sources.quote: In these verbs, the prestem syllable is phonetically more intense or stronger than the stem syllable is. [p. 8] ... in these categories [nouns and postpositions], the vowel of the stem is of greater intensity than the vowel of the prestem syllable when both are low tone. [p. 9] ... I have proposed that in Hare there is a single binary metrical foot erected starting at the stem. In verbs the foot is labelled left strong and in nouns it is labelled right strong. [p. 16] ... I am not sure just what the phonetic correlate of what I am calling intensity is. It is definitely not pitch ... It appears to have to do with intensity and perhaps duration. [fn. 5]

sources.note: Hare (a North Slavey dialect) is a tone language with a predictable prominence ('intensity') pattern anchored to the stem: in verbs the syllable immediately before the stem (prestem syllable) is stronger than the stem; in nouns and postpositions the stem syllable is stronger than the prestem syllable. Analysed as a binary foot built at the stem, left-strong in verbs, right-strong in nouns. Correlate is intensity/duration, not pitch. Author speculates the verb pattern arose from lexicalisation of a final low boundary tone (Hyman 1977). Read in full; no acquisition needed.

In Hare the stem-tone assimilates to that of the suffix, but in Bearlake and Slavey there is no such assimilation … Mountain appears tonally identical with Bearlake.

tone.quote: In this paper, we examine the prosodic structure of Y/N Q’s and focus constructions in three related Dene/Athabaskan tone languages spoken in North American: Navajo, Dene Sų́łíne, and North Slavey (Deline), known for their complex polysynthesis … Navajo has been argued to lack any kind of intonational prominence, but the northern languages show more typical prominence marking. In this study we lay out the difference associated to the demarcation of boundaries and prominence: duration and the acoustic correlates of pitch accent events associated with focus and YN/Q’s and boundary marking.

sources.note: A methodological retrospective built entirely on Rice's 1970s fieldwork on 'FGH Dene' = the Fort Good Hope variety of North Slavey ('often called Hare', p. 690).
